name: Fatima Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the livestock lead at Greenhollow, a co-operative farm owned by about forty members, me included with one small share. We've 70 dairy cows, a bit of wheat and oats, and a farm shop that sells our milk and yoghurt. I'm in the parlour by half five, then calves, then feed planning, then whatever meeting the co-op has dreamed up that week. I love the calves. I could do without the meetings, though I'd defend them to anyone.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being the person in between. The board wants costs down, the younger members want everything organic, and the cows just want to be milked on time. My partner Sam works at the council roads depot, and our two, Yusuf and Mira, are eleven and eight. I do use one of those AI chat tools now and then, mostly to tidy up grant forms, because I hate writing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. That suits a co-op, honestly, because co-ops are slow anyway. The cows don't care either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the members' meeting I'd say good, now can we stop talking about robots and spend the robot milker fund on the calf shed. That's 40,000 sitting there while the calves winter under a leaking roof. I'd say it nicely, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's about as safe as a farm job gets, and Sam's depot job is council work, so that's steady too. What nags me is the milk price and feed costs, and a board that wants costs down at every single meeting. If the board ever decides a livestock lead plus a relief milker is too much, they'll look at the relief hours first, then at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push hard for the calf shed at the spring meeting. At home we'd keep saving 200 a month and finally fix Mira's bike. I'd use the AI chat tool a bit more, for the feed budget as well as grant forms, once I've seen it give sensible numbers twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. There's a small knot about the board and the milk cheque, but it's the knot I've had for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the milk cheque look like these days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Down about eight percent on last year, and feed's up. We get by because the farm shop yoghurt makes a better margin than the milk does. If the shop had a bad year, I'd stop sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace, our part-time milker. Grace is 58 and has worked with us for nine years. Every cost-cutting conversation at the co-op ends with somebody looking at the relief milker's hours. I'd fight for Grace before I'd fight for the calf shed.

say: Let's stop talking about robots and spend the **40,000 robot milker fund** on the calf shed.
The calves are wintering under **a leaking roof** while that money sits there.
think: My job is about as **safe** as farm work gets, and Sam's council job is steady.
What nags me is **the milk price**, feed costs and a board that wants costs down at every meeting.
The **relief milker's hours** would be first in line for any cut.
do: Pushes for the **calf shed** at the spring members' meeting.
Keeps saving **200 a month** at home.
Tries the AI chat tool on **the feed budget** once it has given sensible numbers twice.
feel: **Mostly settled**, with an old knot about the milk cheque and the board's cost-cutting.
S0.quote: Every cost-cutting conversation at the co-op ends with somebody looking at the relief milker's hours.
fieldNote: Fatima sees her own and her partner's jobs as **secure**, so her unease comes from the co-op's finances.
The milk cheque is down and the **farm shop's yoghurt** holds things together.
Her protectiveness of **Grace**, the older part-time milker, came up before any question about her own pay.

steps.text: Keep milking at half five and running the calves as now
Push the co-op to spend its 40,000 fund on a calf shed
Keep saving 200 a month at home
Try the AI chat tool on Greenhollow's feed budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. So the cows are fine and the clipboard isn't. That's awkward, because the clipboard is half of what makes me livestock lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the co-op I'd say this is our chance: let the AI do the grant forms and the feed sums and give people more time with the animals. I'd also say we must decide together what happens to anybody whose hours shrink, before the board decides it for us. I'd say that to the union rep too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the bit of my job that pays the lead allowance is the planning, and planning is exactly what the software takes. Feed budgets, herd records, grant forms, the rota. The board would ask why they're paying a lead rate to someone who mostly milks, and I could drop to a herd worker's wage, maybe 3,000 a year less, with a mortgage to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI properly for feed plans in the first few months, once I've seen Fernley do it, so I'm the one running it and not the one replaced by it. I'd ask the union to put a clause in our agreement that nobody's pay is cut because of software for at least two years. At home we'd keep saving 200 a month and put off the new kitchen again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with things to do. I don't mind the change, I mind finding out about it in a board paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace again, though Grace is safer than me in this one, which is funny. Grace milks and doesn't touch computers, and nobody's building a robot milker by next year. It's the people in the middle, me and Owen in the farm office, who'd feel it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say my job's not going, but my title might be. Sam would say a title never paid a bill, and he'd be right, except the lead allowance does. Then we'd do the sums at the kitchen table like we always do.

say: This is our chance to let AI do **the grant forms** and feed sums and free time for the animals.
We must decide together what happens to anyone whose **hours shrink**, before the board decides for us.
think: The part of my job that earns **the lead allowance** is the planning, and that's what the software takes.
I could drop to a herd worker's wage, about **3,000 a year** less, with a mortgage to pay.
do: Takes over **feed plans with AI** within months, once the Fernley co-op has shown it works.
Asks the union for a **two-year no-pay-cut clause**.
Keeps saving 200 a month and puts off **the new kitchen**.
feel: She minds less about the change than about learning of it **from a board paper**.
S1.quote: The bit of my job that pays the lead allowance is the planning, and planning is exactly what the software takes.
fieldNote: Fatima saw that the new card falls on **the planning half** of her job, the half that pays her lead rate.
The cows, and Grace's milking, are safer than **her own title** in this picture.
As usual she'd move **once it's proven nearby**, and wants the union to buy time first.

steps.text: Take over Greenhollow's feed plans with AI once Fernley has proven it
Ask the union for a two-year no-pay-cut clause
Keep saving 200 a month towards the mortgage
Put off the new kitchen until the lead allowance is settled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, five for the hands. Our board takes two years to choose a paint colour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the members we have three years between the AI and the robots, and that's exactly the time a co-op needs if we start now. I'd put a motion to the spring meeting to set up a planning group for it. Online I'd say the same thing, that farms owned by the people who work them have to plan together or the big dairies will plan for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my mornings in the parlour are safe until about 2031, but my feed planning and the grant forms are gone in 2028. That's maybe a third of my week, and it's the part that gets me the title of livestock lead. Then in 2031 the big robot dairies start selling milk cheaper than we can, and I don't know if forty members can agree fast enough to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd start using the AI properly for feed plans, not just grant forms, because by then it would be proven and I'd be daft not to. I'd get the planning group going and push the co-op to start a robot fund now, even if it means the calf shed waits again. At home we'd put the 200 a month toward the mortgage instead of savings, to get the balance down before Sam's job at the roads depot goes the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. If I've got a list and a meeting date, I can carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Sam's job. What happens at the roads depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam drives a gritter and patches potholes, so that's hands-on too, and the council would probably wait for the robots. But the depot's rotas and orders would go to the AI in 2028, and his supervisor already talks about cutting staff. So we'd have two jobs on the same three-year clock, which is the bit I'd stare at the ceiling about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Grace, the part-time milker you worried about before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace would be 63 by 2031, close enough to her pension that a co-op could carry her for two years if we wanted to. I'd make sure the planning group put Grace's job in writing as the first thing we protect. If a co-op can't look after a woman who's milked its cows for nine years, what's the point of a co-op?

say: We have **three years** between the AI and the robots, exactly the time a co-op needs if we start now.
Farms owned by the people who work them **have to plan together**, or the big dairies will plan for us.
think: My parlour mornings are safe until about 2031, but **the feed planning** and grant forms go in 2028.
Then **the big robot dairies** undercut us, and I don't know if forty members can agree fast enough.
do: Starts using **AI for feed plans** as soon as it's proven.
Sets up a co-op planning group with **a robot fund**, even if the calf shed waits again.
Moves the family's **200 a month** from savings to the mortgage before Sam's depot job is hit.
feel: With a list and **a meeting date** she can carry it.
S2.quote: If a co-op can't look after a woman who's milked its cows for nine years, what's the point of a co-op?
fieldNote: Fatima split her job in two: the **planning** that goes in 2028 and the parlour work that lasts to 2031.
Her real worry is **two household jobs** on the same three-year clock, since Sam's depot work follows the same pattern.
Under pressure she **organises**, and she puts the oldest worker first.

steps.text: Use the AI for Greenhollow's feed plans, not just grant forms
Set up a co-op planning group and a robot fund at the spring meeting
Put the 200 a month toward the mortgage before Sam's depot job changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five and eight years. That's a co-op-sized timeline, just about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where co-ops can actually win, because we'd have time to buy machines together and share them. I'd say it at the members' meeting and on the farmers' forum. I'd also say the government should help small farms buy in groups, not just hand grants to the big estates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd come out of this one all right if I move in the first two years. I'd be 51 when the robots arrive, and a co-op will still need someone who knows the cows to run the machines and spot a sick heifer. The danger is me waiting too long because waiting is what I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the herd health course at the agricultural college in the second year, evenings, once a couple of people I know have done it. I'd push the co-op to share a robot milker with the Fernley co-op down the valley rather than each buying one. We'd keep saving 200 a month and leave the kitchen for another year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared. It's a long enough run-up that I can see myself landing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said waiting is what you always do. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it work somewhere I trust. When Fernley got their first robot weeder, I went and stood in their field for an afternoon before I'd say a word at our meeting. If the AI was running their herd plans by 2032 and the cows looked fine, I'd be first in the queue after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yusuf and Mira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf would be sixteen when the robots came, so he'd be choosing his subjects. I'd tell my son to learn how the machines work and how animals work, both, because nobody seems to know both. Mira would still think it's all about the calves, and I'd let her.

say: This is the version where **co-ops can win**, because we'd have time to buy and share machines.
The government should help small farms **buy in groups**, not just hand grants to big estates.
think: I'd come out all right if I move in **the first two years**, because a co-op needs someone who knows cows.
The danger is me **waiting too long**, because waiting is what I always do.
do: Signs up for an evening **herd health course** in year two, once people she knows have done it.
Pushes Greenhollow to **share a robot milker** with the Fernley co-op.
Keeps saving 200 a month and puts off **the new kitchen**.
feel: The run-up is long enough that she can **see herself landing it**.
S3.quote: I'd tell my son to learn how the machines work and how animals work, both, because nobody seems to know both.
fieldNote: Fatima names her own **habit of waiting** for proof as the main risk here.
She has a clear test: **watch the Fernley co-op** try it first.
The eight years to robots let her picture **running machines** rather than being replaced by them.

steps.text: Take the evening herd health course at the agricultural college in year two
Push Greenhollow to share a robot milker with the Fernley co-op
Keep saving 200 a month and put off the new kitchen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years until a robot can do my job. I'd be 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got no excuse not to get this right, and I'd want the co-op federation to have a plan on paper within two years. In public I'd keep it upbeat. Ten years is enough time to bring the machines in on our terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the risk with ten years is that nobody does anything for eight of them. Our board has put off a new calf shed for six years running, so I know how a long deadline goes. For me personally, 56 with a herd health skill and a share in the co-op doesn't sound too bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the first few years run as normal and use the AI tools when the co-op does. I'd put 40 a month each into education funds for Yusuf and Mira. And I'd join the co-op federation's policy group, because that's where the shared-machine rules would get written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm on the surface, a bit uneasy underneath. Mostly I worry about everyone else putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Grace would be retired by 2039. Who would you worry about instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, funnily enough, the young one who loves robot weeders. He'd be in his thirties and the machines he dreamed about would be the ones doing his job. He thinks he'll be the one running them, but there won't be many of those jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the first years run as normal. Isn't that what you worry the board will do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair. I'd be doing exactly what I complain about. I suppose the difference is I'd be saving and planning on paper, and the board would be doing nothing at all. That's a thin difference, I know.

say: Ten years is **enough time** to bring the machines in on our terms.
The co-op federation should have **a plan on paper** within two years.
think: The risk with ten years is that **nobody does anything** for eight of them, like our board with the calf shed.
For me, being 56 with **a herd health skill** and a co-op share doesn't sound too bad.
do: Lets the first few years run as normal and **adopts AI tools** when the co-op does.
Puts **40 a month each** into education funds for Yusuf and Mira.
Joins the co-op federation's **policy group** to help write shared-machine rules.
feel: **Calm on the surface** and a little uneasy underneath, mostly about other people putting it off.
S4.quote: Our board has put off a new calf shed for six years running, so I know how a long deadline goes.
fieldNote: Fatima expects herself to be fine but distrusts what **a long deadline** does to an organisation.
When I pointed out she'd also wait, she **agreed at once**.
Her worry shifted from Grace to **young Jonah**, whose hopes are tied to the machines that would replace him.

steps.text: Run the dairy as normal and adopt AI tools when the co-op does
Put 40 a month each into education funds for Yusuf and Mira
Join the co-op federation's policy group on shared-machine rules

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sam's job and mine would both be on the same three-year clock, and the co-op couldn't move fast enough before the robot dairies undercut us. What would help is public money for co-ops to buy robots together and keep their people, and a basic income while families like ours adjust.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked what happens to the animals. Everyone talks about jobs. But a cow that's been handled by the same person for years notices when that person's gone.

headlineQuote: A cow that's been handled by the same person for years notices when that person's gone.
portrait: Fatima Walsh, 43, is **livestock lead** at Greenhollow, a members' co-operative dairy, and holds one small share.
She uses AI now and then for grant forms and trusts **co-op votes** and union deals to steer change.
If AI stalls she's **uneasy**, because the milk cheque is down and the board wants costs cut.
Steady disruption makes her **anxious**: software takes the planning that earns her lead allowance, so she'd learn it early.
Fast AGI puts her and Sam's jobs on **one three-year clock**; with more time she'd retrain, though waiting is her weakness.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job and her partner's would be on the same three-year clock.
The co-op **couldn't move fast enough** before robot dairies undercut it.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money for co-ops** to buy robots together and keep their workers.
